items.title: Manchester’s Co-op Live arena evacuated after ‘unknown substance’ released in crowd
items.desc: Police declare major incident after concertgoers at Don Toliver gig report eye and respiratory symptoms One person was taken to hospital and more than 50 were assessed by medics after a substance was let off in the crowd at Manchester’s Co-op Live arena, officials have said. Police declared a major incident after the release of the substance, which was initially thought to be teargas, as they sought to protect the 12,000 people in the crowd at a Don Toliver concert. Continue reading...

items.title: Grieving families getting into debt and doing without memorials due to benefit freezes
items.desc: MPs to discuss bereavement support as financial help for funeral expenses and bereaved families fails to keep pace with costs Bereaved families are borrowing money or forgoing a service with mourners because financial help available from the state no longer covers even half a typical funeral director’s fee. “The funeral expenses payment (FEP) was originally meant to cover the cost of a simple funeral. Today, that is a pipe dream,” said Lindesay Mace, a co-manager of Down to Earth, a funeral costs support service run by the charity Quaker Social Action. Continue reading...

items.title: Cost of renting in Britain to rise twice as fast as buying amid shortage of properties
items.desc: Rents to rise by 14% until at least 2029, Hamptons predicts, as high demand for properties and low supply push up costs for tenants The cost of renting a home in Britain is expected to rise about twice as fast as that of buying one until at least 2029, according to research, with shrinking supply pushing up the prices paid by tenants. Rents on newly agreed lets are forecast to grow by 14.2% between 2026 and 2029, compared with house price growth of 7.2%, according to forecasts from estate agent Hamptons. Continue reading...

items.title: Burnham not ‘backtracking’ on creating closer links with EU, officials say
items.desc: Government wants to let trade deal ‘breathe a bit’, insiders say, after speculation No 10 is dialling back ambitions Andy Burnham is not backtracking or delaying his ambitions to create even closer links with the EU in the wake of a landmark summit in Brussels, the Guardian has been told, after signs of an apparent slowdown in the timetable. The prime minister has promised to set out options for the UK’s long-term relationship with the EU, including the possibility of rejoining, saying last week that these would be outlined later in the year. Continue reading...

items.title: ‘Once installed, there’s no getting rid of it’: what Falklands oil plans mean for its seals, whales and penguins
items.desc: While Argentina and the UK dispute sovereignty over the islands and its vast oil reserves, environmentalists fear for one of the Atlantic’s richest ecosystems From the air, the main Falkland Islands form two large, jagged shapes against the South Atlantic. East Falkland and West Falkland are surrounded by 778 smaller islands and islets east of Patagonia’s southern tip. The archipelago, a British overseas territory claimed by Argentina, is home to large colonies of albatrosses and penguins. Its waters, with those of the Patagonian shelf, provide feeding grounds for sea lions, southern elephant seals and southern right whales. Continue reading...

items.title: MPs urge Miliband to force UK overseas territories to publish public company registers
items.desc: Improvements in corporate transparency ‘essential’ amid ‘outright disregard for the will of parliament’, says cross-party group Ed Miliband is being urged by MPs to use his powers to force overseas territories such as the British Virgin Islands to publish public company ownership registers – almost a decade after parliament voted for transparency. Ahead of a meeting between the foreign secretary and overseas territories this week, a cross-party group of MPs from Labour, the Tories, Lib Dems and Greens wrote to Miliband calling on him to mandate public registers of beneficial ownership of companies. Continue reading...

items.title: Fewer than half in UK will pay TV licence fee within a decade, report warns
items.desc: Analysis for thinktank points to cycle of falling income leading to lower spending on content in ‘spiral of decline’ Fewer than half of households in Britain will pay the BBC’s licence within a decade, according to analysis that warns that the broadcaster’s funding is locked in a “spiral of decline” . With senior BBC figures concerned about the accelerating fall in licence fee sales, the independent projections also warn that the proportion of households paying the levy will further decline to less than a third by 2037-38 should the government persist with the corporation’s current funding model. Continue reading...

items.title: Theresa May’s blast from the past calls Tories back to their unhappy place | Peter Walker
items.desc: Conservatives may instinctively want to push back against closer EU ties, but they have to train their focus elsewhere Anyone who accidentally switched to BBC One at about 9.45am on Sunday to be greeted by Theresa May awkwardly espousing the virtues of Brexit could have been forgiven for thinking they had woken up in around 2018 – and not being especially pleased at the idea. This is one of the problems now facing May’s party. For all that it is a reflex action for Conservatives to push back against closer ties with the EU, Andy Burnham’s decision to pursue such a course plunges them back into their own unhappy place. Continue reading...

items.title: NHS savings drive leaves hospitals in England facing ‘unpalatable’ cuts
items.desc: Exclusive: Thirty-one trusts issue stark warning that cost-cutting demands threaten their ability to function normally Dozens of hospitals are so short of money they may not be able to continue caring for patients and are being forced to make “unpalatable” cuts to services and staff, the Guardian can reveal. Thirty-one health service trusts in England have issued stark warnings that NHS demands for them to make huge budget savings this year threaten their ability to function normally. All have declared that as a threat in the register of risks they have to maintain and publish. Continue reading...

items.title: Russell Brand’s wife vows to abide by prison rules after video controversy
items.desc: Laura Brand says in new video on YouTube she will continue Sunday Service series she started with Brand Russell Brand’s wife, Laura, has promised to “absolutely honour” rules set by the prison where her convicted sex offender husband is being held, in another YouTube video published on Sunday. This week Andy Burnham called on Google to take down a video uploaded to Russell Brand’s YouTube channel last Sunday that contained a statement from the disgraced comedian in prison, where he is serving a 10-and-a-half-year sentence for rape and sexual assaults. items.title: Pip review will call for overhaul rather than scrapping benefit for under-25s
items.desc: Recommendations overseen by Stephen Timms would retain system for all ages, unlike last week’s Milburn review A long-awaited review of the personal independence payment (Pip) system will this week recommend that it is overhauled, a week after another report called for it to be partly scrapped. The final report on Pip by a committee co-led by Stephen Timms, the social security minister, is expected to be published as soon as Tuesday, presenting Andy Burnham with one of his most politically sensitive decisions yet as prime minister. Continue reading...

items.title: UK taxpayers held more than £1tn in offshore tax havens, latest HMRC data shows
items.desc: Figures show recent 10% rise in total held in financial centres such as Jersey and Panama, raising fears over cost to public purse The amount of money UK taxpayers hold in offshore accounts in tax havens has exceeded £1tn for the first time, raising concerns about potential losses to the public purse. HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) data, obtained by the TaxWatch thinktank through freedom of information requests, shows between 2022 and 2024 the value of balances held offshore in tax havens increased by 10%. These were the latest available figures. Continue reading...

items.title: Rivals author Jilly Cooper accused of ‘extensive and deliberate plagiarism’
items.desc: Analysis reportedly finds striking similarities in dialogue and narrative structure between late author’s novel, Prudence, and two of her contemporaries Jilly Cooper has been accused of plagiarising the works of two other novelists. The bestselling author’s fifth romance series novel, Prudence, published in 1978, allegedly includes several plagiarised passages from The Serial by Cyra McFadden and The Franchise Affair by Josephine Tey. items.title: Man who killed three during psychotic episode ‘had been released after catalogue of failures’
items.desc: Alexander Lewis-Ranwell was arrested and let go twice by police in the 48 hours before he killed three men in their 80s in Exeter A man with paranoid schizophrenia who killed three people while experiencing a psychotic episode had been released from custody after a “catalogue of failures” by police and medical professionals, an investigation has found. Alexander Lewis-Ranwell was arrested and released twice by police in the 48 hours before he killed Anthony Payne, 80, and the twin brothers Roger and Dick Carter, 84, in their homes in Exeter in 2019. items.title: ‘Just wrong’: British right distances itself from Trump after Putin ‘friend’ post
items.desc: Reform deputy leader calls Russian leader ‘a murderous dictator’ after US president appears to endorse him Reform UK and the Conservatives have distanced themselves from Donald Trump after the US president posted a photo of himself shaking hands with Vladimir Putin with the caption: “My friend.” The US president had already used the term to describe the Russian president while at last week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, southern China, where he also met the Chinese president, Xi Jinping. items.title: CEO of funding agency for UK science and research criticised by union over cuts
items.desc: Exclusive: Prospect’s Mike Clancy tells Ian Chapman at UKRI that union has ‘lost confidence’ in his leadership A trade union that counts scientists and engineers among its members says it has lost confidence in the leader of the UK’s national funding agency for science and research, citing concerns about plans for major cuts. The letter from Mike Clancy, the general secretary of Prospect, to Ian Chapman, the chief executive of UK Research and Innovation (UKRI), is the latest development in a row over changes in funding for projects and research facilities. items.title: Closer EU ties will give UK say on Brussels decisions, says Ed Miliband
items.desc: Foreign secretary says there is clear case to integrate more closely but does not say if he backs talks on possibly rejoining Closer links with the EU will mean the UK having a say on decisions made by Brussels, Ed Miliband has argued as ministers faced pressure to move further after Friday’s landmark deal with the EU. Any timetable for closer integration, including possible talks about the UK rejoining the EU, remains unclear after the Brussels summit, with Andy Burnham saying he would now “brainstorm” over future ties. Continue reading...

items.title: Theresa May ‘aghast’ at Andy Burnham’s talk about rejoining EU
items.desc: Former PM who opted for minimal ties with bloc says moves towards membership would dominate government’s time Theresa May has said she feels “aghast” at Andy Burnham’s plan for potentially rejoining the EU, arguing in a rare interview that the prime minister should “accept Brexit and move on”. Speaking to the BBC after Friday’s UK-EU summit , at which Burnham secured the biggest step towards renewed ties with Brussels since Brexit, May said that a further move towards membership, as talked about by the PM, would dominate the government’s time. Continue reading...

items.title: UK-EU food deal hailed by British firms: ‘We’re pretty aligned anyway’
items.desc: Exporters welcome end in sight for Brexit checks – but are frustrated that implementation will take so long British producers have broadly welcomed the UK’s deal with the EU, designed to remove the vast majority of physical checks on food, plants and animal products. The sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) deal is expected to benefit Britain’s food exporters and will enable UK delicatessens and other small retailers to import European cheese and wine again, something that became economically unviable because of costly Brexit checks. Continue reading...

items.title: Exquisitely decorated home of Victorian workman David Parr wins blue plaque
items.desc: Working-class man who covered mansions with William Morris’s patterns spent his nights filling his Cambridge terrace house with his own designs As a Victorian working-class labourer, David Parr was paid to spend his days decorating the interiors of private mansions and Cambridge colleges with William Morris’s magnificent designs. But as an artist, Parr chose to spend his nights filling his modest terrace house with the most resplendent decor and exquisite craftsmanship he could create. Continue reading...
